title: Iterative shared divider removes the execute critical path
motivation:
The baseline's 199.837 ns, 156-cell worst path runs through forwarding,
execute, and the ALU before reaching the data-memory address. The ALU
currently contains separate combinational signed and unsigned / and %
expressions, making division a likely source of the extreme logic depth
even for ordinary address calculations. At 5.442 MHz, shortening this
path can outweigh a modest cycle cost on DIV and REM instructions.

even for ordinary address calculations. At 5.442 MHz, shortening this

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the four combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU expressions in the timed
core with one shared, radix-2 iterative quotient/remainder datapath. Run
one compare/subtract iteration per cycle, with signed magnitude conversion
and RV32M-correct divide-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 handling. Keep other ALU
operations, including multiplication, single-cycle. Hold the dividing
instruction and fetch/decode until its result is ready, while allowing
older EX/MEM and MEM/WB instructions to drain; inject invalid EX/MEM
bubbles during the wait. Capture the forwarded operands at divider start
so later writeback or bus stalls cannot change the operands or RVFI data.
Preserve the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions. Removing the deep divide
network from the single-cycle forwarding-to-address path should raise
Fmax enough to improve CoreMark iterations/second despite divider stalls.

Add a divide wait interlock that holds PC and ID/EX without freezing older EX/MEM or MEM/WB work; give data-memory stalls priority where needed.
Wire divider wait and completion into the existing pipeline controls without changing the top-level IO or retirement contract.

title: Serialize division outside the execute combinational path
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz and its 156-cell critical path runs
through forwarding and the combinational ALU. The ALU contains four
synthesizable 32-bit divide or remainder expressions, which put a deep
arithmetic network on the execute result path even for common non-divide
instructions. Its 12,312 LUT4 count is also above the 10,000 target.
CoreMark's timed kernels rely heavily on multiply, while their divisions
are infrequent or by compile-time constants, so a longer DIV/REM latency
should cost much less than the clock-rate gain from removing this path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU logic with one shared
four-iteration restoring divider in a separate sequential module. Each
iteration resolves eight quotient bits with a short chain of eight
subtract/select steps, reusing that hardware for all four operations.
In execute, latch the forwarded operands and operation once, hold the
current ID/EX instruction and fetch PC while division runs, allow older
EX/MEM and MEM/WB instructions to drain, and inject invalid EX/MEM
bubbles until the result is ready. Emit exactly one normal EX/MEM result
on completion and then release the front end. Convert signed operands to
magnitudes before unsigned division, correct quotient and remainder signs
afterward, and handle divide-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 exactly as RV32M
requires. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, carry its existing substituted
arithmetic result through the same short divide handshake, so formal
still exercises pipeline stall and forwarding behavior within its fixed
liveness window. Verify real arithmetic through clocked ALU cocotb tests,
CoreMark cosim, and the unchanged deep formal gate.
Removing the unrolled divide and remainder networks should substantially
shorten the clock path and reduce LUT pressure while preserving the
single-retirement RVFI and memory-stall behavior.

title: Fetch-stage backward-branch and JAL prediction
motivation:
The current fetch PC always advances by four, so every taken branch and
direct jump is redirected from EX and discards the instruction entering ID.
CoreMark contains hot counted loops and direct calls; removing these
predictable control bubbles should improve iterations per cycle without
adding a large table to the already area-heavy FPGA design.

hypothesis.motivation:

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict legal backward conditional branches taken and forward branches not
taken from the fetched instruction's B immediate. Predict every JAL to its
direct target. Only predict an aligned target; misaligned control transfers
must follow the existing trap path. Carry the predicted next PC with the
instruction into EX; compare it with the resolved next PC after forwarding
and correct only on a valid instruction's mismatch. Drive correction to the
actual next PC, including the sequential PC on a trap. JALR remains
sequentially predicted. Gate prediction on a valid imem beat and preserve
correction priority over bus stalls. This targets CoreMark loop and call
bubbles while keeping the predictor off the deep arithmetic path.

title: Narrow the ID/EX flush to control and validity
motivation:
The current champion's 29.788 ns worst path starts at the register file,
passes through execute, fetch redirect and hazard logic, and ends at an
ID/EX operand register. The ID stage clears its entire wide register on a
branch redirect or load-use bubble, so the late flush signal controls the
input mux of every operand and metadata flop. This path limits Fmax while
the existing divider has already removed the much deeper arithmetic path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion's 29.788 ns worst path starts at the register file,

ID/EX operand register. The ID stage clears its entire wide register on a
branch redirect or load-use bubble, so the late flush signal controls the
input mux of every operand and metadata flop. This path limits Fmax while

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change the ID/EX register so flush clears only valid and the decoded
control bits; capture operand values, immediate, instruction and addresses
without a flush-dependent data mux whenever the stage advances. A flushed
instruction then carries no enabled memory, register-write, branch, jump,
or divide action, while its don't-care data cannot affect architectural
state. Keep flush priority over the load-use hold exactly as today, and
retain full reset initialization. The narrower late-control fanout should
shorten the register-file-to-ID/EX path and improve Fmax without adding
cycles or changing the retirement contract. Verify wrong-path and load-use
bubbles under instruction and data bus stalls.

title: Make pipeline squashes valid-bit only
motivation:
The champion's 29.788 ns worst path starts at the register file and runs
through EX, IF, hazard control, and back into the ID/EX register. Fetch
currently substitutes a NOP on a redirect or instruction stall, and ID
clears its entire pipeline payload on a flush. Thus the branch decision
controls the fetched instruction, decode addresses, and all ID/EX data
register inputs in the same cycle. This feedback limits Fmax despite the
iterative divider having removed the old arithmetic path.

Make squashes change only pipeline valid bits, rather than muxing a NOP

Pass io_imemData through the existing combinational fetch bundle; on an
unavailable or wrong-path beat, mark it invalid. Let the ID/EX payload
registers capture or hold their data as before, but clear only ID/EX.valid
on redirect and load-use bubbles. Qualify load-use detection with both
IF/ID.valid and ID/EX.valid. In EX, require ID/EX.valid for redirects and
register zero EX/MEM control for an invalid instruction; qualify memory
requests, EX/MEM forwarding, and memory-stall detection with EX/MEM.valid.
WB already qualifies register writes with MEM/WB.valid, while its retained
data must remain available for forwarding across dmem stalls. Keep the
present PC redirect priority, pipeline depth, and retirement behavior.
The late branch decision then reaches only kill/valid flops instead of

bubble. This should shorten the clock period at nearly unchanged IPC.

title: Bimodal branch prediction with direct jump prediction
motivation:
The current core fetches sequentially until EX resolves each branch or
jump, wasting a fetch/decode slot on every taken control transfer. The
earlier backward-branch/JAL predictor reduced CoreMark cycles from
4,491,817 to 4,259,699, but it was evaluated with the old combinational
divider and its 5.47 MHz critical path. The current 44.515 MHz champion
uses an iterative divider. A small direction predictor can also learn hot
forward branches while preserving a short EX correction path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current core fetches sequentially until EX resolves each branch or
jump, wasting a fetch/decode slot on every taken control transfer. The
earlier backward-branch/JAL predictor reduced CoreMark cycles from
4,491,817 to 4,259,699, but it was evaluated with the old combinational
divider and its 5.47 MHz critical path. The current 44.515 MHz champion
uses an iterative divider. A small direction predictor can also learn hot
forward branches while preserving a short EX correction path.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry PC-indexed bimodal predictor containing a short tag, a
valid bit, and a two-bit saturating taken counter. On an untrained entry,
use the successful backward-taken/forward-not-taken static rule; on a tag
hit, use the counter. Fetch computes the B immediate target for legal
conditional branches and the J immediate target for JAL, selecting that
target when predicted taken and aligned. Predict every aligned JAL taken;
leave JALR sequential. Carry the predicted-taken bit with the instruction.
In EX, repair a conditional branch only when its effective taken outcome
(taken and aligned) differs from predicted taken, using its actual target
or PC+4. The target comes from
the same latched PC and instruction, so branch repair needs no 32-bit
predicted-target comparison on the forwarding-to-fetch path. Preserve the
existing JALR redirect, misaligned-target trap, and RVFI actual next PC.
Train each legal conditional branch once when EX advances, and do not
advance fetch or predictor metadata on a stalled imem beat. Misprediction
correction retains priority over imem and dmem stalls. This should keep
the previously measured loop and JAL cycle savings while learning CoreMark
forward branches at modest area and timing cost.

title: Share branch comparison logic in execute
motivation:
The current champion's 26.552 ns worst path leaves the ID/EX register,
passes through execute branch resolution and fetch prediction, and returns
through fetch/decode control. Execute currently computes equality, signed
less-than, and unsigned less-than as separate 32-bit comparators before
selecting among six branch conditions. The comparison and selection sit
on the redirect feedback path that limits Fmax.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion's 26.552 ns worst path leaves the ID/EX register,
passes through execute branch resolution and fetch prediction, and returns
through fetch/decode control. Execute currently computes equality, signed
less-than, and unsigned less-than as separate 32-bit comparators before
selecting among six branch conditions. The comparison and selection sit
on the redirect feedback path that limits Fmax.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the six branch-condition expressions in EX with a shared equality
check and one unsigned magnitude comparator. Derive signed less-than from
that same result: when the operand sign bits differ, the sign of rs1 is the
signed result; otherwise signed and unsigned less-than are identical.
Decode funct3 only into signed/unsigned selection and result inversion,
with BEQ/BNE using the equality result. Keep forwarding,
branch target generation, misalignment trapping, predictor training, and
RVFI behavior unchanged. This should remove a parallel 32-bit comparator
and shorten the comparison-to-redirect mux, raising Fmax without changing
CoreMark cycle count.

title: Register the fetch to decode boundary
motivation:
The 118.61 fitness champion has a 26.552 ns worst path that starts in the
register file, passes through EX and the direction predictor into fetch,
then returns through decode toward the register file. The current IF/ID
bundle is combinational, so an EX branch correction can affect the fetched
instruction and decode inputs in the same cycle. The prior valid-only
squash experiment retained this combinational stage boundary and did not
improve fitness. A pipeline register at that boundary directly cuts the
feedback path while retaining the successful fetch-side prediction.

hypothesis.motivation:
The 118.61 fitness champion has a 26.552 ns worst path that starts in the
register file, passes through EX and the direction predictor into fetch,
then returns through decode toward the register file. The current IF/ID
bundle is combinational, so an EX branch correction can affect the fetched
instruction and decode inputs in the same cycle. The prior valid-only
squash experiment retained this combinational stage boundary and did not

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one valid-tagged IF/ID pipeline register between the fetch output and
the decoder. Capture the instruction, PC, and predicted-taken bit only when
the imem beat is ready and the front end can advance. Feed decode and the
load-use comparator from this registered instruction. On a load-use or
downstream hold, retain both IF/ID and the fetch PC; on a missing imem
beat, let an older valid IF/ID instruction enter ID/EX and replace IF/ID
with an invalid bubble. On an EX redirect, invalidate the buffered IF/ID
entry immediately and invalidate ID/EX next state when EX can advance;
keep the redirecting EX instruction held during a dmem stall. Give the
corrected PC priority over every bus stall. Qualify controls
from invalid entries so they cannot issue memory requests, train the
predictor, write a register, or retire. Preserve the existing branch
direction predictor, iterative divider, and single-channel RVFI contract.
The added stage costs one cycle of misprediction recovery, but should
shorten the dominant clock path enough to exceed that IPC cost and the
4.6% acceptance margin. Check simultaneous redirect, imem stall, dmem
stall, and load-use cases with the existing formal and cosim contracts.

title: Predictor guided fetch ahead across pipeline stalls
motivation: The current predictor already handles most direct control transfers, but fetch is locked to decode. Every load-use, data-memory, or divide stall stops the fetch PC even when imem can deliver predicted-path instructions. Later imem stalls then leave decode empty. CoreMark retires about 2.92 million instructions in 4.19 million timed cycles with roughly 22% imem backpressure; the available overlap is substantially larger than the remaining branch and return mispredictions.

hypothesis.motivation: The current predictor already handles most direct control transfers, but fetch is locked to decode. Every load-use, data-memory, or divide stall stops the fetch PC even when imem can deliver predicted-path instructions. Later imem stalls then leave decode empty. CoreMark retires about 2.92 million instructions in 4.19 million timed cycles with roughly 22% imem backpressure; the available overlap is substantially larger than the remaining branch and return mispredictions.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Decouple predicted fetch from decode with a two-entry fall-through FIFO holding instruction, PC, and predicted-taken metadata. Keep the existing bimodal and direct-JAL predictor, but let its fetch PC advance and enqueue each accepted imem beat while decode is held by load-use, dmem, or divide stalls. Decode consumes queued instructions during imem stalls. When the FIFO is empty and imem is ready, bypass the incoming beat directly to decode so ordinary zero-wait fetch adds no cycle. Permit one enqueue and one dequeue in the same cycle, including when the FIFO starts full; hold the fetch PC only for imem backpressure or a full FIFO without a dequeue. On an EX correction, discard all younger queued beats, ignore the coincident imem beat, and restart the fetch PC at the resolved target, with correction taking priority over both bus stalls. Store prediction metadata with its instruction and keep EX training and RVFI retirement ordered exactly as before. This predictor-guided lookahead should overlap independent instruction and backend stalls without changing the instruction-memory handshake or relying on cached instruction data.

title: One-hot execute operand forwarding
motivation:
The current champion's 23.309 ns worst path begins at the register file,
crosses execute and a multiplier, and ends at the EX/MEM ALU-result register.
Nearly tied paths cross the same execute rs1 mux before branch correction
reaches fetch and decode. The priority encoded forwarding mux has several
LUT levels before either path's arithmetic; ALU-B adds an immediate mux.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion's 23.309 ns worst path begins at the register file,
crosses execute and a multiplier, and ends at the EX/MEM ALU-result register.
Nearly tied paths cross the same execute rs1 mux before branch correction
reaches fetch and decode. The priority encoded forwarding mux has several
LUT levels before either path's arithmetic; ALU-B adds an immediate mux.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decode forwarding priority into mutually exclusive one-hot source enables
for the ID/EX value, EX/MEM result, and MEM/WB result. Form each execute
operand with a parallel masked OR tree, and fold ALU immediate selection
into the second operand's one-hot network so immediate instructions bypass
the rs2 forwarding mux entirely. Keep the original source priority, x0
behavior, raw forwarded rs2 for stores, branch comparisons, divider launch,
and RVFI operand values. The shorter operand selection depth should improve
Fmax on both near-tied path families while retaining the same CoreMark cycle
count and retirement behavior.

title: Use a flip-flop bank for the integer register file
motivation:
The current register file is inferred as two Gowin BSRAM blocks. The worst
timing paths launch at those BSRAM read outputs and continue through EX to
either the multiplier result or branch and predictor control. Register-file
read latency and placement therefore limit both tied 23.3 ns paths. The
core has substantial LUT and flip-flop headroom under its area target.

title: Tagless XOR-indexed bimodal branch predictor
motivation:
The existing 64-entry direction predictor stores a valid bit, ten tag bits,
and a two-bit counter per entry. Its tag read and comparison add logic to
fetch, while frequent PC-index collisions replace useful hot-branch state.
A trace-level model of the canonical CoreMark binary finds 529,588 timed
conditional branches and about 45,007 direction errors with this table.
The predictor should use its FPGA storage and fetch timing budget more
efficiently on these common conditional branches.

title: Register write-qualified bypass matches before execute
motivation:
The champion's Gowin report has nearly tied 22.347 ns and 22.343 ns
setup paths. Both start at a producer's destination-register bit,
pass through forwarding selection, and then reach either the EX/MEM
ALU-result register or the fetch PC through branch resolution. Thus
pipelining only multiplication would leave the branch path limiting
Fmax. The prior combinational one-hot forwarding attempt did not help;
its register comparisons still sat in front of execute. Moving those
comparisons across a pipeline boundary addresses both paths together
without adding a branch or data-dependency cycle.

forwarding path. Preserve EX/MEM over MEM/WB priority and x0
suppression, including misaligned-access and misaligned-jump traps.

extra execution or retirement cycle. This should shorten both tied

and beyond the 4.6% acceptance margin. The prototype also passed all
53 single-retirement formal checks.

title: Banked predicted-path fetch lookahead
motivation:
The registered IF/ID boundary ties fetch progress to decode, so ready
instruction-memory beats are lost during load-use, data-memory, and divide
stalls. A previous two-entry predicted-path queue reduced the timed
CoreMark run from 4,208,030 to 3,970,277 cycles, but its 48.668 MHz
placement lost more Fmax than it gained in cycles. The current flip-flop
register file has since shortened the execute critical path. A dynamic
trace also shows only 13,735 JALR returns in the timed region, so perfect
return prediction alone cannot clear the 4.6% acceptance threshold.

instruction, PC, and existing predicted-taken bit in a fixed register bank;
the predicted fetch PC advances whenever the window has space, even while
decode is held. IF/ID consumes the oldest buffered beat on an imem stall,
with direct bypass from imem when the window is empty and ready, preserving
ordinary one-instruction-per-cycle operation. Support simultaneous pop and
push, including a full-window pop, with bank-local write enables and a
small head/tail pointer rather than shifting wide payloads. On EX
correction, invalidate queued wrong-path beats and restart the predictor
PC at the resolved target; correction wins over bus stalls. Keep the
current bimodal direction table, aligned direct-JAL prediction, registered
IF/ID boundary, RVFI ordering, and nret=1 interface. Limit late EX
correction to validity/pointer control so queue data muxes do not join the
register-file-to-ALU timing path. The deeper window should recover more
instruction stalls than the earlier two-entry attempt while banked storage
and the faster register file limit the Fmax cost, improving the product of
CoreMark iterations per cycle and Gowin Fmax.

title: Retime the fetch and execute feedback loops
motivation:
The 161.91 champion has three nearly tied setup paths: 20.000 ns from
a registered forwarding match through a DSP multiplier to EX/MEM,
19.995 ns from the fetch PC through the tagged BHT back to the PC, and
19.908 ns from a forwarded branch operand through redirect control to
the wide ID/EX reset. Improving only one path would barely move Fmax.
A structural retiming of these feedback loops can remove combinational
work from all three without slowing ordinary one-cycle instructions.

hypothesis.motivation:

19.995 ns from the fetch PC through the tagged BHT back to the PC, and

the wide ID/EX reset. Improving only one path would barely move Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Retime the two long feedback calculations across existing pipeline
boundaries. In execute, capture post-forwarding operands and operation
for MUL, MULH, MULHSU, and MULHU, then produce the exact RV32M result
from registered inputs on the next cycle. Hold ID/EX and fetch for
that one cycle, inject an invalid EX/MEM bubble, and retire the multiply
exactly once; let older stages drain and give a dmem stall priority.
Ordinary ALU, branch, and memory instructions keep their current latency.

In fetch, register the BHT hit and direction lookup for the sequential
PC+4 one cycle ahead. A single alignment-valid bit follows sequential
PC advances; use the registered direction only while it is aligned
with the current PC. Otherwise apply the existing backward-taken
static rule to the current fetched instruction. A direct target or EX
redirect clears that alignment bit until the sequential lookup catches
up.
Thus the current PC no longer traverses the BHT read and tag comparison
before updating. On a redirect, invalidate IF/ID and ID/EX by clearing
their valid bits, rather than resetting their wide payloads through
the late forwarded-branch path. Preserve PC redirect priority over both
bus stalls and keep all side effects qualified by pipeline validity.

These register boundaries should move the tied DSP, BHT, and redirect
paths below the next timing limit. The occasional multiply bubble and
first-instruction static prediction after a transfer should cost less
throughput than the resulting Fmax gain; verify the net score with the
vendor flow and unchanged CoreMark and formal contracts. Keep the
ALTOPS substitution on the same multiply handshake in formal.

title: One-entry predicted-path fetch skid buffer
motivation:
The registered IF/ID stage loses ready instruction beats whenever decode
is held by a load-use, data-memory, or divide stall. Earlier two- and
four-entry predicted-path queues reduced CoreMark cycles, but their extra
payload banks and control lowered Gowin Fmax enough to lose fitness. The
current 68.134 MHz critical path is in execute, so a much smaller fetch
buffer is the best chance to recover stalled fetch cycles without moving
that path or substantially changing placement.
